title: The self split in two — husband and wife, the whole world (1.4)
hook: the lonely self makes itself fall in two, and the two halves chase each other through every kind of creature
tomorrow: the self is dearer than a son

segments.voice: Yesterday, aham asmi: the self alone said I am, then felt fear, then loneliness, and wanted a second.

People still say it at weddings: my other half. It sounds like a greeting card. In the Brihadaranyaka, one of the oldest Upanishads, it isn't a greeting card at all. It's a creation story. The self was alone, and lonely. It wanted a second, and there was no second anywhere. So it did the only thing it could. It used itself.
screen: `MY OTHER HALF.` → `ALONE, AND NOTHING ELSE ANYWHERE.` → `IT USED ITSELF.`

segments.voice: The self, the text says, was as big as a man and a woman holding each other. It made itself fall in two, and from that came husband and wife. The Sanskrit plays on its own words here: the verb for fall is pat, and husband and wife are pati and patni. Then the text quotes the sage Yajnavalkya, whom we'll meet properly in two days: each of us, he used to say, is like half of something split. Translators argue over the exact object, half a shell or half a split pea, but the picture is the same. You are the half, and the empty space beside you is the shape of the other. The two halves joined, and humans were born. Then the story turns strange and wide. She thinks: he made me from himself; how can he join with me? I'll hide. She becomes a cow; he becomes a bull. She becomes a mare; he, a stallion. A she-goat, a goat. A ewe, a ram. And on and on, the text says, down to the ants. Every pair of creatures in the world comes out of that chase. At the end the self knows: I am this whole creation, because I poured it out of myself. So the story is about a marriage, and about much more than a marriage. Everything that comes in twos, wanting and wanted, is the one self looking for itself. Look back at this week: the dreamer, then deep sleep. The horse as the cosmos. Death's hunger making a world. Breath staying clean. I am. And today, the half.
screen: `IT MADE ITSELF FALL IN TWO.` · `PAT, PATI, PATNI.` · `SHE HIDES; HE FOLLOWS, DOWN TO THE ANTS.` · `I AM THIS WHOLE CREATION.` · then, large: `YOU ARE THE HALF.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who completes something in you: a partner, a friend, a sibling, a child, someone gone. Notice the space beside you that only they fill, and don't fix or say anything; just let the space be there, and let it be full. If no one comes to mind, rest in the line itself, and notice how much of the world comes in pairs.
Ardha, half. In the Brihadaranyaka, the one self falls into two, and every pair of creatures comes from that split; each of us, Yajnavalkya says, is ardha, half of something split.
Your line: you are the half. Tomorrow, a line about love that sounds like a trap. See you then.

howItsDone: Students read this as part of the Brihadaranyaka's creation account in chapter one; in many Hindu weddings the couple is spoken of as two halves of one, and the wife is called ardhangini, the half of the body.
